title: Checkpoint: Building It Is a Chain of Verifications
summary: The construction phase comes down to one discipline: nothing counts as done, paid or accepted until someone independent has verified it. This checkpoint lesson revisits the hardest ideas of the phase, from survey control to closeout, as one chain of proofs the owner controls.
body:
Building is not a sequence of activities. It is a sequence of proofs: each step is allowed to start only when the step before it has been verified by someone who did not do the work, and the owner's job is to keep that chain unbroken.

Recall

Q. In Week 122, what did Marco say an owner must document before terminating a contractor?

A. The contractual ground, the notices given and the cure periods allowed, the state of the work and the records on site, all checked by counsel, because a termination that skips a contractual step can turn the owner into the party in breach.

Q. In the Week 121 post-mortem, what did changes after sign-off have in common?

A. Each looked small on its own, none was re-checked against the whole design, and together they removed the margin the original design relied on.

Q. What is a long-lead register?

A. A list of every item whose manufacture and delivery takes longer than the time available, with its order date, approval date and delivery date tracked, so that procurement does not quietly set the opening date.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the checkpoint for Phase 12, Building It. Over thirteen weeks you have walked from the survey peg to the occupancy certificate: site work and dewatering, shallow and deep foundations, concrete in the plant and in the field, steel and prefabrication, procurement, quality, payment, changes and claims, closeout, a reverse-engineered building, a construction post-mortem and leading as owner. It is a lot of material. This week compresses it into the few ideas that decide whether a building comes in safe, on budget and defensible, and tests whether you can say them aloud under pressure.

The reason to compress is practical. On site you will not have time to recall thirteen lessons. You will have one question in front of you, usually from someone who wants a decision today. If you hold the phase as one chain, you can place that question in a second and know what proof is missing.

The chain: verify, then release

In plain English: every important thing on a building site is held until it is proven, and the person who proves it is not the person who wants it released.

The professional framing has five links. First, the setting out: the surveyor's control points are checked before anything is built off them, because every later error inherits a wrong grid. Second, the ground: the geotechnical engineer confirms the bearing stratum or the pile capacity before load goes on it. Third, the hold point: an inspection and test plan, or ITP, names the points where work must stop until a named inspector signs, for example reinforcement checked before concrete is placed. Fourth, payment: money is released against work verified in place, not against work claimed. Fifth, completion: the building is accepted only when it has been tested as a working system and the records exist to prove it.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A floor slab is ready to pour on a Thursday. The reinforcement inspection is a hold point. The inspector is delayed until Friday. The concrete is booked, the pump is booked and the crew of 12 is on site. The contractor asks to pour and inspect from photographs. Standing down costs about 15,000 dollars in idle crew, pump and rebooking. A slab poured over misplaced steel, discovered later, can cost several hundred thousand dollars to test, assess and repair, if it can be repaired at all. The proof costs 15,000 dollars. Its absence can cost twenty or thirty times that and a reputation. You hold the pour.

Say that out loud now.

Time, money and records are the same chain

The second hard idea of the phase is that schedule, cost and records are not three systems. They are one system seen from three sides.

The professional framing: the schedule of values is the contractor's price broken into lines it will bill against. If early lines are priced high, which is called front-loading, the contractor is paid ahead of the work and the owner carries the risk if it fails. Retainage, a percentage held back from each payment until completion, is a commercial term in most contracts and a statutory holdback in some places; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Changes and delay claims depend on notice: most contracts make written notice within a fixed period a condition precedent to recovery, so a claim with no notice may be lost however good its merits. And every one of these depends on contemporaneous records: daily reports, photographs, test results and signed inspection sheets written at the time, not reconstructed later.

A second worked example. A contractor claims 40 days of delay for late owner approvals. The contract requires notice within 21 days of the event. The daily reports show the approvals were late by 25 days, and notice was given 30 days after the first late approval. On a typical clause, the claim for the first few days may be time-barred, and the claim for the rest stands only as far as the critical path was actually affected, which a time impact analysis must show. Your records decide what you pay. If your own decision log shows approvals issued on time, the claim collapses. If you kept no log, you are arguing from memory against a contractor who kept one.

Closeout is where the chain is cashed

The third hard idea: completion is a legal and financial event, not a date on a schedule. Substantial completion usually means the building can be used for its intended purpose, which often starts warranties, releases part of the retainage and moves risk of loss and insurance to the owner. Final completion means the punch list is closed and the documents are handed over. Between the two sits the commissioning record: functional performance tests and integrated systems tests proving that fire alarm, smoke control, generator, elevators and life-safety systems work together. Latent defects, hidden faults that surface later, are governed by the contract's warranty period and by limitation periods in law; verify those against the primary source before you rely on them.

How the best do it

The strongest builders treat inspection and testing as a planned production activity, not an interruption. Before work starts on each trade, they agree the ITP with the designers and inspectors, book the hold points into the look-ahead schedule and give each one a named person. Large tall-building contractors also run a first-of-a-kind mock-up for each repeated element, so the inspection standard is set once and then copied. A small developer can copy this: insist that the contractor's look-ahead schedule shows every hold point with a name and a date, and review it weekly.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: how costs are coded during construction, between building, equipment and site works, can affect later depreciation; ask a tax adviser before the cost codes are fixed. Liability: an owner who directs means and methods can take on liability the contract gave to the contractor, so direct outcomes, not methods. Banking: the lender's monitor verifies the same chain, so a clean chain is a fast draw. Governance: approval authorities say who may release a hold, a payment or a change. Estate: the closeout records are part of the asset an heir or trustee inherits. Exit: a buyer prices the building partly on the completeness of its records.

Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record and the special inspector, for hold points on structure; the commissioning authority, for integrated testing.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is schedule pressure converting a hold into a formality. The control is a written rule, issued before mobilisation, that only the named inspector can release a hold point, that photographs are never a substitute and that the owner will pay the cost of a delay rather than accept unverified work.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner judges progress by what he can see on a site walk. A full floor of concrete looks like progress. Whether it is progress depends on the test results, the inspection sheets and the cylinder breaks, which you cannot see from the walkway. Ask for the paper before you praise the work.

Callback

In Week 40, Priya taught the in-balance test: the money left must cover the cost to complete. This phase supplies the evidence that test needs. A lender who trusts your records funds on time, and the records come from exactly the chain of verifications in this lesson.

Recap

Building is a chain of proofs: setting out, ground, hold points, payment and completion. Nothing is done, paid or accepted until someone independent verifies it. Schedule, cost and records are one system, and closeout is where the whole chain is cashed.

Next: Ford on Failure Forensics: a composite case of a pour paid for before it was proven.
checklist: Every hold point in the inspection and test plan has a named inspector and a date in the look-ahead schedule.
I have issued a written rule that only the named inspector can release a hold point.
The schedule of values has been checked for front-loading before the first payment.
I know the notice period for claims in the contract and keep a decision log that shows when I issued approvals.
Daily reports, photographs and test results are filed within one working day.
I know what substantial completion triggers in my contract: warranties, retainage, insurance and risk of loss.
Commissioning tests are scheduled before the occupancy inspection, not after.
A buyer could audit the building from its records without visiting the site.
head: Field checklist
speak: Building is a chain of proofs, not a list of activities. Each step starts only when the step before it has been verified by someone who did not do the work. The chain has five links: the survey control, the ground, the hold points in the inspection and test plan, payment against work verified in place, and completion proved by integrated testing. Schedule, cost and records are one system: a front-loaded schedule of values pays the contractor ahead of the work, a claim without timely written notice can be lost on the clause alone, and contemporaneous records decide what gets paid. Closeout is a legal and financial event that starts warranties and moves risk to the owner. When a contractor asks me to pour before the inspector arrives, I compare the cost of waiting with the cost of being wrong, and I almost always wait. Only the named inspector releases a hold.
terms: Hold point — a step in the inspection and test plan at which work must stop until a named inspector has inspected and signed it off.
Front-loading — pricing the early lines of a schedule of values high so the contractor is paid ahead of the work actually in place.
Substantial completion — the stage at which the building can be used for its intended purpose, usually triggering warranties, retainage release and a transfer of risk and insurance to the owner.

hostile.q: You are three weeks behind and the inspector is a day late. Why are you paying a crew to stand around instead of pouring?
hostile.a: Because a pour over unverified steel is not progress; it is an unpriced risk. Standing down costs about 15,000 dollars and one day. A defect found later can cost many times that, may force testing or demolition and would delay the whole frame. I will recover the day in the look-ahead schedule, and I have asked for the inspector to be booked a day earlier on every remaining floor so this does not recur.

title: The Floors That Were Paid For Before They Were Proven
summary: This is a composite example of a construction phase that failed one reasonable shortcut at a time: low cylinder breaks noted and not acted on, reshores pulled early to recover the schedule, and draws that followed the bills. Taken through the seven forensic steps, it shows how a building can be both late and unsafe because the chain of verification was broken at the points that felt cheapest to skip.
body:
This is a composite example. Nobody on this project decided to build an unsafe structure. They decided, one week at a time, that a test result could wait, a reshore could come out early and a bill could be paid on trust, and the sum of those decisions was a frame that had to be shored, tested and partly rebuilt.

Recall

Q. What are the five links in the chain of verification from yesterday's lesson?

A. Survey control, the ground, hold points in the inspection and test plan, payment against verified work in place, and completion proved by integrated testing.

Q. What is reshoring?

A. Placing temporary props back under a recently cast slab after the formwork is removed, so that the young concrete and the floors below share the load of the floors still being built above until the concrete is strong enough.

Q. What does a low break mean in concrete testing?

A. A cylinder or cube test result below the specified strength at the specified age. It is a trigger for investigation, such as further tests or cores, not a verdict on its own.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, real collapses during construction have often happened when formwork or shores were removed before the concrete could carry its load. I am using a composite here so that I do not put a number or a quote into a real investigation that I cannot verify. The pattern is real; the project is assembled from it, and every figure is a hypothetical round number. Roman sits in today because this failure also ran through the money: the same week the tests were ignored, the payments ran ahead.

1. Timeline

Month 1: a contractor wins a fixed-price contract for a reinforced concrete frame, with a programme of one floor every 10 days. Month 2: the schedule of values is approved with formwork, mobilisation and general conditions priced heavily at the front. Month 4: the frame falls 3 weeks behind after a wet spell. Month 5: the contractor moves to a 7-day floor cycle to recover, which means stripping forms and moving reshores sooner. Month 5: two sets of 7-day cylinders come back below the expected trend. Month 6: a 28-day result on one floor is low. Month 6: a site engineer notes visible cracking and excess deflection at mid-span on a lower floor. Month 7: the structural engineer of record is told. Cores are taken, the floors are back-propped, work stops for 9 weeks, and two bays are strengthened. Month 9: the contractor, already paid ahead, enters a dispute and then insolvency.

2. Key decisions

Four decisions carried the failure. Approving a front-loaded schedule of values without challenge. Accepting a faster floor cycle without asking the structural engineer to re-check the stripping and reshoring sequence. Treating the low 7-day results as noise because "they will come up by 28 days". And continuing to certify payments at the contractor's claimed percentage while the monitor's notes showed concern.

3. Assumptions

The team assumed concrete gains strength on a calendar, regardless of temperature and mix. It does not; strength gain depends on the mix, the curing and the weather, which is why stripping should be decided by verified strength, not by the day of the week. They assumed reshoring was the contractor's business alone. Temporary works are the contractor's design responsibility under most contracts, but a change to the cycle changes the loads on permanent structure, which the engineer of record must see. And they assumed a fixed-price contractor carries the cost of its own mistakes. It does, until it cannot pay.

Say that out loud now.

4. Incentives

This is where the shortcuts came from. The contractor faced liquidated damages, a fixed daily sum payable for late completion, so every day recovered was money saved. The site team was praised for floor-cycle speed. The owner's representative was measured on schedule, not on quality. The lender's monitor was paid to report, not to stop work. Nobody in the room was rewarded for waiting for a test result. When every incentive points at the calendar, the calendar wins unless a rule stands in the way.

5. Warning signs ignored

The signs were in writing. The schedule of values put a large share of the contract in the first quarter of the work, a classic front-loading pattern. The cycle change came with no revised temporary works design. The 7-day results were below the trend that would reach specified strength by 28 days. The monitor's report used the words "billing appears ahead of progress". A site engineer recorded cracking. Each sign alone had an innocent explanation. Together they described a frame being loaded faster than it could carry and a contractor being paid faster than it was building.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the decision to keep the faster cycle after the first low results arrived. Up to that week, stopping cost a few days and some testing. After it, three more floors had been cast onto lower floors whose strength was unproven, so the investigation had to cover the whole stack, and the repair had to wait for the load above it to be propped down to the foundations.

Notice what made this point hard to see. Nothing dramatic happened that week. The results were a few points low, the cycle looked impressive and the payments matched the bills. The point of no return in most construction failures is a quiet week in which a stop would have been cheap and inconvenient, and continuing felt like the professional choice. If you remember one thing from this case, remember that the cheapest moment to stop is almost always the moment it feels most unnecessary.

7. Root cause

The root cause was not bad concrete. It was that nobody owned the hold. The contract named tests but no hold points tied to stripping or loading; the test results went to a filing system rather than to a person with authority to stop work; and the payment process trusted the contractor's percentage complete. The chain of verification existed on paper and had no one standing at its links.

Roman's money view, in hypothetical round numbers. The contractor's price was 20,000,000 dollars. By month 6 the contractor had been paid 9,000,000 dollars against work the monitor later valued at 7,000,000 dollars. Strengthening, testing, back-propping and a 9-week stop cost the owner about 2,500,000 dollars, and a replacement contractor priced the remaining work 3,000,000 dollars above the original balance. Retainage of 10 percent, about 900,000 dollars, was the only cushion. Against a combined gap of roughly 7,500,000 dollars, it was a small one.

The prevention rule

Rule 123: never let schedule pressure release a hold. Formwork stripping, reshore removal and loading are tied to verified strength and the engineer of record's sequence, a low result stops loading until it is resolved, and no payment certifies work the independent monitor has not verified in place.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that test results arrive in an inbox and leave as a file. The control is a result-to-action route: every test result goes to a named person within one working day, with a written trigger that says what result stops what work.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes a fixed-price contract transfers the risk. It transfers the cost of the contractor's errors only while the contractor is solvent. Once it fails, the owner owns the building, the defects and the gap.

Callback

In Week 40, I took you through a composite in which draws followed bills and a contractor failed. This case adds the structural half of that story. Front-loading is not only a credit problem; it is the same pressure that makes a contractor run the frame faster than its concrete can follow.

Recap

A composite frame failed through four ordinary decisions: a front-loaded price, an unreviewed faster cycle, ignored low results and payments on trust. The root cause was that nobody owned the hold. Rule 123 ties stripping and loading to verified strength and payment to verified work.

Next: Quincy on The Money: where construction money leaks, and how to plug each leak.
checklist: The stripping and reshoring sequence is approved by the engineer of record before the first slab, and re-approved if the cycle changes.
Stripping and loading decisions are tied to verified strength, not to a calendar day.
Every concrete result reaches a named person within one working day, with written triggers.
A low result stops further loading on that pour until it is investigated and resolved.
The schedule of values has been compared with an independent cost breakdown before approval.
No payment certifies work the monitor has not verified in place.
Incentives on site include quality and safety measures, not only floor-cycle speed.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite example. A concrete frame fell behind, and to recover, the contractor moved to a faster floor cycle, stripping forms and moving reshores sooner, with no revised temporary works design. Early cylinder results came back low and were treated as noise. Cracking was noted. Meanwhile the schedule of values was front-loaded and payments followed the contractor's percentage, not verified work. When the engineer of record finally saw it, cores were taken, floors were back-propped, work stopped for weeks and the contractor, paid ahead, failed. The root cause was not bad concrete. It was that nobody owned the hold: tests went to a file, not to a person who could stop work. Rule 123: never let schedule pressure release a hold. Stripping and loading follow verified strength, a low result stops loading, and no payment certifies unverified work.
terms: Liquidated damages — a fixed sum per day, agreed in the contract, that the contractor pays the owner for late completion instead of proving actual loss.
Temporary works — the formwork, shoring, reshoring, propping and other structures needed only to build the permanent works safely.
Back-propping — installing props through several floors down to a firm base so that a weak or overloaded slab no longer carries load while it is investigated or repaired.

hostile.q: As your lender, I see the contractor has billed 45 percent and the monitor says 35. Why should I keep funding?
hostile.a: You should fund only the 35 percent the monitor has verified, less retainage, and I have already instructed my cost consultant to certify on that basis. I am also asking the contractor to re-base its schedule of values against an independent breakdown, and the gap stays unpaid until the work exists. If the in-balance test is affected, I will deposit the shortfall before the next draw.

rule: Rule 123: Never let schedule pressure release a hold; tie formwork stripping, reshore removal and loading to verified strength and the engineer of record's sequence, stop loading on any low result until it is resolved, and certify no payment for work the independent monitor has not verified in place.

title: Checkpoint: The Five Places Construction Money Leaks
summary: Construction budgets rarely fail in one blow. They leak through five channels: front-loaded payments, changes, delay, stored materials and an unfinished closeout. This checkpoint lesson prices each leak in hypothetical round numbers and shows how it reaches cost, return and the lender's ratios.
body:
A construction budget almost never breaks in one blow. It leaks, steadily and quietly, through five channels, and an owner who watches those five channels every month will see an overrun months before it becomes a crisis.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 123?

A. Never let schedule pressure release a hold. Stripping, reshore removal and loading follow verified strength and the engineer of record's sequence, a low result stops loading until resolved, and no payment certifies work the monitor has not verified in place.

Q. What is cost to complete?

A. An independent estimate of everything still to be spent to finish the project, including remaining construction, soft costs, interest and contingency. It is not the same as budget remaining.

Q. What is a development spread?

A. The gap between the yield on cost of a project and the market cap rate for the finished asset. It is the margin that pays for development risk.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, during construction your equity is usually spent first and the loan funds after it. That means every dollar of overrun is either new equity from you, a deposit to keep the loan in balance, or a draw on contingency that should have been there for real surprises. Overruns do not stay on site. They move your return, your lender's ratios and, if you have signed a cost-overrun guarantee, your personal balance sheet. Knowing where money leaks lets you put a meter on each channel.

Leak one: paying ahead of the work

In plain English: if you pay for more than has been built, you are lending the contractor money with no security.

The professional framing is overbilling. The contractor's schedule of values may be front-loaded, or a monthly pay application may claim a higher percentage complete than exists. The difference between billed and verified work is an unsecured exposure. Retainage, the percentage held back from each payment, is a cushion against it, typically 5 to 10 percent in commercial practice, though statutory holdbacks apply in some places; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

A worked example, hypothetical. Contract sum 10,000,000 dollars. Billed to date 4,500,000 dollars, verified in place 3,800,000 dollars. Retainage at 10 percent of billed is 450,000 dollars, so net paid is 4,050,000 dollars. Your real exposure is net paid less verified work: 4,050,000 minus 3,800,000, or 250,000 dollars paid for work that does not yet exist. That figure is the one to report every month. If it rises three months running, the contractor's cash flow is depending on your money.

Leak two: changes

Every change order carries its direct cost plus overhead, profit and, often, time. Change markup is commercial practice set by the contract, commonly a stated percentage for overhead and profit on the contractor's own work and a smaller one on subcontracted work. The leak is not the markup; it is the change that arrives without a price agreed first and is settled at the end, when you have no leverage.

A second worked example. A change for added waterproofing has a direct cost of 80,000 dollars. The contract allows 10 percent overhead and profit, so 8,000 dollars, plus the contractor claims 6 days of time-related cost at 5,000 dollars a day, 30,000 dollars. Total 118,000 dollars, of which only 80,000 dollars is the thing you asked for. Before approving, ask whether the 6 days are on the critical path. If the time impact analysis shows the waterproofing runs in parallel with work that was already critical, the time portion may fall to zero and the change costs 88,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

Leaks three, four and five: delay, stored materials and closeout

Delay is the most expensive leak because it charges you twice. You pay the contractor's time-related costs, such as site staff, cranes and site facilities, if the delay is compensable, and you pay your own carrying costs: interest on the loan, insurance, project management and lost rent or delayed sales. On a hypothetical project with a 30,000,000-dollar loan at 7 percent drawn on average to half, a month of delay costs about 87,500 dollars in interest alone, before any other carry.

Stored materials are equipment or materials paid for before they are installed, on site or off site. Paying for them can protect price and schedule, but you are paying for something you may not own if the supplier fails. The control is evidence of title, insurance naming you, and segregation and marking of the goods, as Week 114 and Week 117 covered.

Closeout leaks money through an unfinished punch list, missing warranties and missing commissioning records. If retainage is released in full at substantial completion, the contractor has little reason to finish the last two percent. Hold back an amount clearly larger than the cost of the open items, a common commercial practice is around 1.5 to 2 times their value, until they are closed and the documents are handed over.

How the leaks reach return and the lender

Take a hypothetical project with total cost 50,000,000 dollars and stabilised net operating income of 3,500,000 dollars, a yield on cost of 7 percent. If the five leaks together add 2,500,000 dollars, cost rises to 52,500,000 dollars and yield on cost falls to about 6.67 percent. Against a market cap rate of 5.5 percent, the development spread falls from 1.5 points to about 1.17 points, a loss of more than a fifth of the margin that pays you for the risk. If 3 months of delay also push stabilisation back, the levered internal rate of return falls further, because the same profit arrives later on more equity. And at the lender's end, a higher loan balance from capitalised interest can tighten the debt service coverage ratio at take-out.

The contingency meter

One more meter ties the five leaks together. Compare how much of your construction contingency has been used with how much of the work is complete. Suppose a hypothetical contingency of 2,500,000 dollars, 5 percent of cost, and the project is 40 percent complete. If 1,500,000 dollars, or 60 percent of the contingency, is already committed, you are spending your protection faster than you are building. The risks that remain are not smaller just because the early ones are behind you; envelope, services and commissioning still carry plenty. A useful habit is to ask your cost consultant each month for the contingency used, the contingency committed but not yet spent, and a fresh view of the risks still ahead. When the first number runs ahead of percentage complete for two months, you call a cost review before the third.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, a construction project shows as equity at cost, but you should carry a second number beside it: contingent liabilities. A completion guarantee or cost-overrun guarantee does not appear as a debt until it is called, and when it is called it can be larger than the equity you put in. Write down each guarantee, its cap if it has one and the overrun that would trigger it. Then keep your liquidity floor, the cash you never commit, large enough to fund a realistic overrun without selling anything in a hurry. A licensed adviser is required before you act on how much that floor should be.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is watching the budget instead of the exposure. The budget can look intact while you have paid ahead of the work. The control is a monthly report with three numbers: verified work in place, net paid and cost to complete, reconciled by an independent cost consultant.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner approves changes to keep the job moving and agrees their price at the end. Price every change before the work, or at minimum cap it and record the basis, and decide the time question by analysis, not by negotiation.

Callback

In Week 51, Quincy taught earned value: comparing the value of work done with the money spent and the schedule planned. The five leaks are earned value made practical. Overbilling, changes, delay, stored materials and closeout are the reasons earned value and actual cost drift apart.

Recap

Construction money leaks through paying ahead, unpriced changes, delay, stored materials and closeout. Measure exposure, not budget. A few percent of overrun can remove a fifth of the development spread, and guarantees put that risk on your personal balance sheet.

Next: LEX on The Rules: the contract and statutory rules that decide who pays on site.
checklist: My monthly report shows verified work in place, net paid and cost to complete side by side.
I calculate the exposure of net paid over verified work every month and watch its trend.
Every change is priced, or capped with a recorded basis, before the work proceeds.
Time claimed on a change is tested against the critical path before I agree it.
I know my monthly carrying cost of delay in interest, insurance and lost income.
Stored materials are paid only with evidence of title, insurance and segregation.
Closeout retention is held above the value of open items until they and the documents are delivered.
Every guarantee I have signed is listed on my personal balance sheet as a contingent liability.
head: Field checklist
speak: Construction money leaks through five channels. First, paying ahead of the work: my exposure is net paid minus verified work in place, and I report it every month. Second, changes: the leak is not the markup, it is the change priced at the end, when I have no leverage, and the time portion that has not been tested against the critical path. Third, delay, which charges me twice, in the contractor's time-related costs and my own interest and carry. Fourth, stored materials, which I pay for only with proof of title and insurance. Fifth, closeout, where I hold back clearly more than the open items are worth. These leaks reach the return fast: on a hypothetical 50 million dollar project, 2.5 million of overrun cuts yield on cost from 7 to about 6.67 percent and removes more than a fifth of the development spread. And any guarantee I have signed makes it personal.
terms: Overbilling — billing for more work than has actually been completed, so the owner pays ahead of the work in place.
Time-related costs — the contractor's costs that grow with time on site, such as supervision, cranes, site facilities and insurance, usually the basis of a delay claim.
Contingent liability — an obligation that becomes a real debt only if a future event happens, such as a guarantee being called.

hostile.q: You say your budget is intact. Why should I believe you are not already overspent?
hostile.a: Because I do not report budget alone. Each month my cost consultant gives me verified work in place, net paid and an independent cost to complete. This month net paid exceeds verified work by 250,000 dollars, which is inside retainage, and cost to complete is within the undisbursed funds with contingency to spare. I will send you the reconciliation and the three months before it so you can see the trend.

title: Checkpoint: The Four Rules That Decide Who Pays on Site
summary: Most money fights on a building site are settled by four kinds of rule: notice and time bars, payment security such as liens and holdbacks, the definition of completion, and the law on hidden defects. This checkpoint lesson revisits each as a concept, then compares how Canada and Guyana approach the point.
body:
On a building site the facts are usually argued, but the outcome is usually decided by four kinds of rule: whether notice was given in time, who is secured for payment, what completion legally means and how long a hidden defect can be claimed. Know those four and you know where every dispute will end.

Recall

Q. What is the exposure figure Quincy wants reported every month?

A. Net paid to the contractor minus the value of work verified in place. It measures how much you have paid for work that does not yet exist.

Q. What is a condition precedent in a contract?

A. An event or step that must happen before a right or obligation arises, such as written notice that must be given before a claim can be made.

Q. What is a time impact analysis?

A. A method of inserting a delay event into the schedule to measure how far it actually moved the critical path and the completion date.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will rarely win a construction dispute by being more right about the engineering. You win or lose by whether a notice was served, whether a payment was protected, whether the building was legally complete and whether a defect claim was brought in time. These are rules you can manage in advance. This lesson teaches concepts and how to think. It does not tell you what any statute requires where you build. Verify every rule against the primary source before you rely on it, and take legal advice on the contract you actually sign.

Rule one: notice and time bars

In plain English: if the contract says tell me in writing within so many days, and you do not, you may lose the right entirely.

The professional framing is the time bar: a clause making timely written notice a condition precedent to a claim for time or money. Standard forms differ. Some international forms are strict; some North American forms are more forgiving or allow late notice where the other party was not prejudiced. Courts in different places treat strict time bars differently, and some apply doctrines that can soften them. You cannot rely on softening. Treat the clause as written.

A worked example, hypothetical. Your contract requires notice of a claim within 28 days of the contractor becoming aware of the event. The contractor discovers unforeseen rock on day 1 and gives notice on day 40. On a strict reading, the claim for that rock is lost, whatever its merit. As owner, you do not celebrate. You check whether your own conduct, such as directing work to continue without objection, could be argued to have waived the bar, and you keep your responses in writing so that position stays clear.

The owner's side of the same rule matters as much. Many contracts also time-bar the owner: claims for defects, back-charges or liquidated damages may require notice too. Put every notice period, in both directions, on one page in your project file.

Rule two: payment security

Many jurisdictions give contractors, subcontractors and suppliers a statutory right to register a claim, often called a lien, against the land they improved if they are not paid. Many also require the owner to hold back a percentage of each payment, a holdback, for a period after completion so that unpaid subcontractors have something to claim against. Some places add prompt-payment rules with fixed payment periods and fast adjudication. The details, the percentages and the deadlines differ by place and change over time; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

The owner's discipline is the same everywhere: obtain lien waivers or releases with each payment, confirm title is clear before each draw, hold the statutory holdback where one applies, and never pay a contractor in a way that leaves a subcontractor unpaid and able to claim against your land. Paying twice, once to the contractor and again to release a lien, is one of the most common owner losses in construction.

Where statute gives little protection, the contract and the market supply it instead: a payment bond from a surety that pays unpaid subcontractors, a performance bond or letter of credit against contractor default, and joint cheques or direct payment rights for critical trades. These are commercial instruments, and their terms vary. Read what each one actually covers and when a claim must be made under it.

Say that out loud now.

Rule three: what completion means

Completion is a defined term, and the definition is the rule. Substantial completion in most forms means the work is complete enough to use for its intended purpose, sometimes with a monetary test as well. It can start warranty periods, stop liquidated damages, release part of the retainage and transfer insurance and risk of loss. Some statutes define completion for lien and holdback purposes in their own terms, which may differ from the contract's. Read both definitions and know which clock each one starts.

A second worked example, hypothetical. Your contract says substantial completion triggers the release of half of a 10 percent retainage on a 20,000,000-dollar contract, which is 1,000,000 dollars. The contractor certifies substantial completion while the fire alarm is not yet integrated with the smoke control. You cannot occupy, because the authority will not issue occupancy without a working life-safety system. Under most definitions, a building you cannot lawfully use for its purpose is not substantially complete. You reject the certificate in writing, cite the definition and list what is missing.

Rule four: hidden defects and limitation periods

A warranty in the contract, often one year for correction of defects, is a contractual promise to return and fix. It is not the end of the contractor's liability. Latent defects, faults that could not reasonably be discovered at completion, are usually claimable under the general law for a period set by limitation statutes, which may run from discovery rather than completion and may have a long-stop. These periods differ widely by place; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. The owner's control is records: the closeout package, the commissioning results and the as-built drawings are your evidence when a defect appears years later.

Two Systems

A conceptual comparison only; verify against primary source. Canada's construction law is largely provincial. Several provinces have construction or builders' lien statutes with mandatory holdbacks, and some have added prompt-payment and adjudication regimes in recent years [unverified — confirm independently]. Limitation periods are also provincial and vary. Guyana's legal system descends from English common law, so contract terms and general principles of contract, negligence and limitation carry much of the weight, and an owner there should ask counsel directly whether any statutory lien, holdback or prompt-payment regime applies to building work and what limitation periods govern a defect claim [unverified — confirm independently]. The practical lesson is the same in both: where statute gives less protection, the contract must give more, through clear notice clauses, retention, bonds and documented payment releases.

Professional sign-off required: a construction lawyer admitted in the jurisdiction of the site, for the contract, the notice regime and lien compliance.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is managing the work and forgetting the clocks. The control is a single notice and deadline register, maintained weekly by your project manager and reviewed monthly by counsel, listing every time bar, holdback period, warranty start and limitation trigger in both directions.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner answers notices by telephone. A call is not a notice under most contracts. Reply in writing, by the method the contract specifies, to the address it specifies, and keep proof of delivery.

Callback

In Week 77, LEX taught precedence and notices in standard contract forms. This phase showed those clauses at work on a real site: the rock, the delay, the payment and the completion certificate. The clause you skimmed at signing is the clause that decides the claim two years later.

Recap

Four rules decide who pays: notice and time bars, payment security through liens and holdbacks, the definition of completion and the limitation period for hidden defects. Keep one register of every clock, reply in writing and take local legal advice, because each rule varies by place.

Next: Quincy on The Numbers: a pay application and a delay cost worked line by line.
checklist: I have a one-page list of every notice period in the contract, in both directions.
Every notice I send or receive is in writing, by the contract's method, with proof of delivery.
Lien waivers or releases are collected with each payment and title is checked before each draw.
I know whether a statutory holdback applies where I build, and its period, confirmed by local counsel.
I have read both the contract's and any statute's definition of completion and know which clock each starts.
Warranty start dates and latent defect limitation periods are recorded in the closeout file.
A construction lawyer admitted where the site is has reviewed the notice and payment clauses.
head: Field checklist
speak: Four kinds of rule decide who pays on a building site. First, notice and time bars: if the contract makes timely written notice a condition precedent, a late claim can be lost on the clause alone, and many contracts time-bar the owner too. Second, payment security: many places give unpaid contractors and suppliers lien rights against the land and require the owner to hold back part of each payment, so I collect waivers and check title before every draw to avoid paying twice. Third, completion is a defined term: substantial completion can start warranties, stop liquidated damages and move risk, and a building I cannot lawfully occupy is usually not substantially complete. Fourth, hidden defects are claimable for a limitation period that may run from discovery. All of this varies by place, so I keep one register of every clock and take local legal advice.
terms: Time bar — a contract clause making timely written notice a condition precedent to a claim, so that a late notice can defeat the claim.
Holdback — a percentage of each payment that an owner must retain for a period, often under a statute, to protect unpaid subcontractors and suppliers.
Limitation period — the time allowed by law to start a legal claim, after which the claim is usually barred.

hostile.q: Your contractor says you waived the notice clause by letting them keep working on the rock without objecting. Did you?
hostile.a: I do not believe so, and my records are the answer. Each instruction to continue was in writing and expressly reserved my rights under the notice clause. I will have my construction counsel review the correspondence, because waiver depends on the facts and on the local law, and I will not concede or argue the point until that review is done.

title: A Pay Application and a Delay, Worked Line by Line
summary: Two calculations sit under almost every construction month: what to pay against a pay application, and what a delay really costs. This lesson works both forward, step by step, with hypothetical round numbers and units, so you can check a certificate and price a delay yourself.
body:
If you can check a pay application line by line and price a week of delay from both sides of the contract, you can sit in any construction finance meeting and know whether the number in front of you is right.

Recall

Q. What does substantial completion commonly trigger?

A. The start of warranty periods, the end of liquidated damages, the release of part of the retainage and the transfer of insurance and risk of loss to the owner, depending on the contract's own definition.

Q. What is a stored material?

A. Equipment or material paid for before it is installed, held on site or off site. It should be paid only with proof of title, insurance and segregation.

Q. What is the in-balance test?

A. The requirement that undisbursed loan plus equity still to come covers the full cost to complete before any further draw.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will sign or approve a payment every month for the life of the build. A payment certificate is arithmetic, and arithmetic errors move real money: a percentage complete a few points high, retainage on the wrong base, a stored item paid twice. And every time someone says "we are two weeks late", the cost of that sentence needs a number on both sides of the contract. Both calculations take ten minutes when you know the order of the steps. Every figure below is hypothetical and round.

Part one: checking a pay application

In plain English: list what has been built, add what has been delivered and protected, take off what you hold back, take off what you already paid, and the rest is what is due.

The professional framing follows the usual order of a payment application form. Step 1, the schedule of values with each line's value and percentage complete. Step 2, materials presently stored. Step 3, total completed and stored to date. Step 4, retainage. Step 5, total earned less retainage. Step 6, less previous certificates. Step 7, current payment due.

LineScheduled valueClaimed completeValue claimed
General conditions1,000,000 dollars40 percent400,000 dollars
Substructure2,000,000 dollars100 percent2,000,000 dollars
Frame4,000,000 dollars50 percent2,000,000 dollars
Envelope3,000,000 dollars10 percent300,000 dollars
Total10,000,000 dollars4,700,000 dollars

The contractor adds 200,000 dollars of windows stored on site, so total completed and stored is 4,900,000 dollars. Retainage at 10 percent of that is 490,000 dollars. Total earned less retainage is 4,900,000 minus 490,000, which is 4,410,000 dollars. Previous certificates total 3,600,000 dollars. The current payment claimed is 4,410,000 minus 3,600,000, which is 810,000 dollars.

Now verify. The lender's monitor walks the frame and counts 9 of 20 floors complete, which is 45 percent, not 50. Frame value falls to 4,000,000 times 0.45, or 1,800,000 dollars, a reduction of 200,000 dollars. The windows are on site, but the delivery note names the supplier, not the contractor, and there is no bill of sale. You exclude them until title is shown. Revised completed and stored: 4,900,000 minus 200,000 for the frame, minus 200,000 for the windows, which is 4,500,000 dollars. Retainage at 10 percent is 450,000 dollars. Earned less retainage is 4,050,000 dollars. Less previous certificates of 3,600,000 dollars, the payment due is 450,000 dollars, not 810,000.

Say that out loud now.

Two more checks before you sign. First, the general conditions line. It is billed at 40 percent while the contract time elapsed is, say, 35 percent. That is close, but if it ran well ahead of time elapsed, it would be a front-loading signal. Second, the cumulative test: total paid after this certificate, 4,050,000 dollars, should sit below verified work in place, 4,500,000 dollars. It does, by the 450,000 dollars of retainage, so your exposure is negative, which is where you want it.

Part two: pricing a delay from both sides

In plain English: a delay costs the contractor time-related money, costs you carrying money and lost income, and the contract decides who bears which.

A second worked example. The frame is 6 weeks late.

Step 1, the contractor's time-related costs per week: site management 20,000 dollars, tower crane 8,000 dollars, site facilities and temporary services 4,000 dollars. Total 32,000 dollars a week. For 6 weeks, 192,000 dollars. If the delay is compensable, meaning caused by the owner's risk events, you pay this, subject to proof.

Step 2, your own carrying cost per week. Loan interest: an average drawn balance of 20,000,000 dollars at 7 percent a year is 1,400,000 dollars a year, divided by 52, about 26,900 dollars a week. Builder's risk insurance extension, about 2,000 dollars a week. Your project management and consultants, about 3,000 dollars a week. Total about 31,900 dollars a week. For 6 weeks, about 191,400 dollars.

Step 3, deferred income. If the building would have earned net operating income of 2,600,000 dollars a year once stabilised, that is 50,000 dollars a week. A 6-week slip pushes that start back by 6 weeks, deferring about 300,000 dollars. Deferred is not lost forever, but it is lost for the life of the investment's timing, and it lowers your internal rate of return.

Step 4, compare the three cases. If the owner caused the delay, the owner pays steps 1, 2 and 3: about 683,400 dollars. If the delay is excusable but not compensable, such as severe weather where the contract gives time but not money, each side bears its own costs: the contractor about 192,000 dollars, you about 491,400 dollars. If the contractor caused it, the contractor bears its own costs and pays liquidated damages, the agreed daily sum. At 10,000 dollars a day for 42 days, that is 420,000 dollars, which is less than your 491,400 dollars of carry and deferred income. Liquidated damages are a pre-agreed estimate, set when the contract was signed, and they often cap what you can recover. Concurrent delay, where both parties caused delay at the same time, is treated differently by different contracts and courts; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Part three: what the certificate does to the loan

One last step links the certificate to the lender. Before the draw goes in, run the in-balance test with the corrected figures. Suppose the hypothetical project's remaining cost to complete, from your cost consultant, is 6,500,000 dollars of construction, including retainage still to be released, plus 800,000 dollars of soft costs and interest and 400,000 dollars of contingency: 7,700,000 dollars in all. Undisbursed loan is 7,500,000 dollars, and equity is fully spent. The loan is out of balance by 200,000 dollars, and the lender will want that deposited before it funds the 450,000 dollars you just certified. Notice that the contractor's original claim of 810,000 dollars would have made the problem look smaller this month and larger next month. Correct certificates give the lender, and you, the true position early, when it is cheapest to fix.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is signing a certificate on the contractor's percentages. The control is an independent check of every line by your cost consultant or the lender's monitor, with stored materials excluded until title, insurance and segregation are proven.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sets liquidated damages low to win a good price, then finds the daily rate covers less than his own interest. Before signing, calculate your real weekly carry and lost income and set the rate from that figure, within what local law allows as a genuine pre-estimate.

Callback

In Week 117, Quincy taught pay applications, retainage and lien waivers, and in Week 118, Marco and Petra taught excusable, compensable and concurrent delay. Today joins them: the pay certificate is the monthly record of what has been earned, and the delay calculation is what that record costs when it falls behind.

Recap

Check a pay application in seven steps and verify the percentages and stored materials before you sign; here the claim fell from 810,000 to 450,000 dollars. Price a delay as contractor time cost, owner carry and deferred income, then let the contract decide who bears each part.

Next: Marco in The Room: the full mock site meeting for this checkpoint.
checklist: I check every pay application in the seven-step order before I approve it.
Each percentage complete is verified by my cost consultant or the lender's monitor.
Stored materials are excluded until title, insurance and segregation are proven.
I compare the general conditions line with contract time elapsed as a front-loading check.
I know my weekly carrying cost of delay and my weekly deferred income.
My liquidated damages rate was set from my real carry and lost income.
For each delay I record whether it is excusable, compensable or concurrent and why.
head: Field checklist
speak: I check a pay application in seven steps: the schedule of values with each line's percentage, materials stored, the total completed and stored, retainage, earned less retainage, less previous certificates, and the payment due. Then I verify. In my hypothetical, the monitor counted 45 percent of the frame, not 50, and the stored windows had no proof of title, so the payment fell from 810,000 dollars to 450,000. For a delay I price three things: the contractor's time-related cost, here 32,000 dollars a week; my own carrying cost, about 31,900 dollars a week in interest, insurance and management; and deferred income, 50,000 dollars a week. Then the contract decides who pays which. If the contractor caused it, liquidated damages of 10,000 dollars a day may cover less than my real loss, which is why I set that rate from my own numbers before signing.
terms: Payment certificate — the document, issued by the owner's representative or consultant, that certifies how much is due to the contractor for a period.
Compensable delay — a delay for which the contractor is entitled to both more time and more money, usually because the cause is an owner risk.
Excusable delay — a delay for which the contractor gets more time but no extra money, such as some weather or force majeure events.

hostile.q: Your certificate is 360,000 dollars below my application. Are you trying to starve my cash flow?
hostile.a: No. I have paid every dollar the independent monitor verified. The frame is 45 percent complete by floor count, not 50, and the windows will be paid on the next certificate the day you send a bill of sale, insurance naming us and confirmation they are segregated. If you disagree with the floor count, walk it with the monitor this week and I will reissue the certificate if the count changes.

title: Mock Meeting: The Monthly Site Meeting With Three Problems on the Table
summary: This is the full mock meeting for the construction checkpoint. You chair a monthly owner's meeting with the contractor, the engineer of record, the lender's monitor and the cost consultant, and three problems arrive: a low concrete break, a delay claim and an early request for substantial completion. The lesson gives the lines to say, the lines never to say and the question behind each request.
body:
The monthly site meeting is where the owner either holds the chain of verification or quietly lets it go. Run it as a decision meeting, keep every answer tied to a record, and leave with each problem owned, dated and written down.

Recall

Q. In yesterday's pay application, why did the payment fall from 810,000 to 450,000 dollars?

A. The monitor counted the frame at 45 percent, not 50, and the stored windows had no proof of title, so both were taken out before retainage and previous certificates were applied.

Q. What is the question behind the question?

A. The real concern or aim that sits under what someone actually asks, which you answer if you want to settle the matter rather than only the words.

Q. What is a recovery schedule?

A. A revised schedule, usually from the contractor, showing how lost time will be made up through resequencing, extra resources or longer hours, with the cost and risk of each measure.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the mock meeting for the Phase 12 checkpoint. In the room: the contractor's project manager, the structural engineer of record, the lender's monitor, your cost consultant and your commissioning authority, the independent party who will test the systems at the end. You chair. The project is in month 14 of an 18-month programme. Three items are on the agenda, and each is a test of whether you will hold the chain under pressure. Read the lines aloud as you go.

Before you walk in, hold your state. Sit before others arrive, put your agenda and the three relevant records on the table, and decide in advance that you will not decide anything without a document in front of you. Composure in this room comes from preparation, not from personality.

The night before

Read four things before this meeting, and only four. The latest test register, with every result against its trigger. The look-ahead schedule, with every hold point and its named inspector. The notice register, so you know which claims have been notified and when. And your own decision log for the last two months, because any claim about late approvals will be argued from it. Then write three lines on a card: the decision you need from each agenda item, the record that will decide it and the person who owns the answer. You will not read from the card in the room. Writing it is what puts the answers in your head, so that when someone pushes for a quick yes, you already know what proof is missing and can say so calmly.

Item one: the low break

The contractor opens: "The 28-day result on Level 9 came back at about 85 percent of specified strength. It is one cylinder set and the others are fine. We need to strip Level 10 tomorrow to keep the cycle."

The question behind the question: will the owner let the calendar overrule a test?

Say: "Thank you for raising it the day it came in. Level 10 stays propped until the engineer of record tells us in writing what this result means. Until then, no additional load goes onto Level 9."

Turn to the structural engineer: "What do you need to give us an answer, and by when?" The engineer asks for cores and a review of the mix tickets and curing records. Say: "Then please confirm the coring plan today, and we will meet again when the results are in. Contractor, please show a revised look-ahead schedule that keeps the other work moving around Level 9."

Never say: "It is probably fine; one set is not a pattern." You may be right, and if you are, the cores will say so in a few days. If you are wrong, you have said it on the record.

Stay silent after you ask the engineer what is needed. The first person to fill that silence with an opinion usually anchors the room. Let the engineer set the plan.

Say that out loud now.

Item two: the delay claim

The contractor continues: "We are submitting a claim for 30 days of delay and about 960,000 dollars, because your approvals on the façade shop drawings were late."

The question behind the question: has the contractor run out of float and is it looking for the owner to fund a recovery, or for a reason to avoid liquidated damages?

Say: "We will review it properly. Please send the notice reference, the dates you say approvals were due and issued, and a time impact analysis showing how those dates moved the critical path. My cost consultant will check the time-related costs against the records."

Turn to your own records. Your decision log shows the façade submittals arrived incomplete twice and were returned within the contract's review period each time. Do not argue that in the meeting. Say: "Our log shows two resubmissions. We will put our dates beside yours in writing so we are working from the same facts."

Never say: "That is ridiculous" or "We will never pay that." You have not seen the analysis. A flat refusal hardens the claim, and if part of it is valid you will have to walk the words back.

Never say, either: "Fine, let us split it." Splitting a claim before it is analysed rewards the size of the ask, not its merit.

Item three: the early completion request

The contractor closes: "We expect to certify substantial completion in five weeks. We would like half the retainage released then."

The question behind the question: is the contractor short of cash, and does it want to shift insurance and risk to you before the life-safety systems are proven?

Turn to the commissioning authority: "What has to be true for this building to be usable for its purpose?" The answer: integrated testing of fire alarm, smoke control, generator transfer and elevator recall, witnessed, plus the authority's occupancy inspection.

Say: "We will recognise substantial completion on the contract's definition, which means the integrated tests are passed and occupancy is lawful. Please put the integrated test dates in the schedule now, five weeks before you want the certificate. If the tests pass, the retainage release follows the contract."

Never say: "Let us just agree a date." The date is a consequence of evidence, not a negotiation.

Closing the meeting

Read back the actions with names and dates: cores on Level 9 with the engineer's written opinion; the claim documents from the contractor and the owner's comparison of dates; integrated test dates in the schedule. Ask the lender's monitor: "Is there anything in today's items that affects your next report?" The monitor will note the low break. That is fine. A lender who hears it from you first trusts you more, not less. Send the minutes the same day.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk in this room is deciding on the spot to keep the mood good. The control is your rule, stated at the start of the project, that every decision in this meeting is made against a record and confirmed in the minutes, and that anything without a record is an action, not a decision.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner tries to be the most technical person in the room. You are not the engineer, the analyst or the commissioning authority. Your job is to ask each of them the question only they can answer, set the date and hold the line until they do.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught acknowledge, bridge, answer for hostile questions. Every line today uses it. You thank the contractor for raising the break, bridge to the record that will decide it, and answer with an action and a date. The technique you practised in Phase 1 is the one that holds a site meeting together.

Recap

Three problems, one method. A low break stays propped until the engineer answers in writing. A delay claim is answered with a request for its analysis and your own dated records. Substantial completion follows integrated testing, not a negotiated date. Every action has a name and a date, and the minutes go out the same day.

Next: Kema on the Checkpoint: the mock interview, the recording and the rules so far.
checklist: I arrive first, with the agenda and the record for each item on the table.
No load goes onto a pour with a low result until the engineer of record answers in writing.
A delay claim gets a request for notice, dates and a time impact analysis, not an opinion.
I put my decision log's dates beside the contractor's in writing.
Substantial completion is tied to integrated testing and lawful occupancy, scheduled early.
I ask the lender's monitor at the end whether anything affects the next report.
Every action has a name and a date, and the minutes are sent the same day.
head: Field checklist
speak: In the monthly site meeting I chair a decision meeting, not a briefing. When the contractor wants to strip a floor above a low concrete break, I thank them, keep it propped and ask the engineer of record what is needed and by when, then stay silent and let the engineer set the plan. When the contractor tables a delay claim, I do not call it ridiculous and I do not split it. I ask for the notice, the dates and a time impact analysis, and I put my own decision log's dates beside theirs in writing. When the contractor asks for substantial completion and retainage in five weeks, I ask the commissioning authority what makes the building usable, and I tie the date to integrated testing and lawful occupancy. I close by reading back every action with a name and a date, ask the lender's monitor what affects the next report, and send minutes the same day.
terms: Commissioning authority — the independent party who plans, witnesses and records the testing of building systems to prove they work individually and together.
Integrated systems test — a witnessed test showing that linked systems, such as fire alarm, smoke control, generator and elevators, respond correctly together to an event.
Float — the amount of time an activity can slip without delaying the project completion date.

hostile.q: As your lender's monitor, why should I not flag your project as at risk after a low concrete result and a large delay claim?
hostile.a: You should report both, and I would rather you heard them from me. The low result has a coring plan and the floor above stays propped until the engineer of record gives a written opinion. The claim has not been analysed yet; we have asked for the time impact analysis and our records show two incomplete resubmissions. The cost to complete includes a provision for both. I will send you the engineer's opinion and our claim comparison as soon as each exists.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Checkpoint: Building It
summary: This is the checkpoint for the construction phase. Answer six mock interview questions aloud, record a three-minute explanation of how an owner controls a building under construction, score it from 1 to 5 on accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question, and then read every rule so far aloud and restate it.
body:
You have learned the construction phase when you can explain, out loud and without notes, how an owner keeps the chain of verification intact from the survey peg to the occupancy certificate. Today you test that, record it and write down the score.

Recall

Q. In the mock site meeting, what did you do when the contractor asked to strip the floor above a low concrete break?

A. Kept it propped, asked the engineer of record what was needed and by when, stayed silent while the engineer set the plan, and asked the contractor for a revised look-ahead schedule around the affected floor.

Q. What does Rule 123 say?

A. Never let schedule pressure release a hold. Stripping, reshore removal and loading follow verified strength and the engineer's sequence, a low result stops loading until resolved, and no payment certifies work the monitor has not verified.

Q. From Week 9, what is a checkpoint for?

A. To test whether you can perform what you have read, aloud and under a little pressure, and to give you a dated score to beat next time.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Kema. During construction you will be questioned by a lender's credit officer, a monitor, a contractor's commercial manager and, one day, a buyer's due diligence team. They do not test whether you have read about hold points or retainage. They test whether you can explain, in plain words and under a little pressure, how you kept control of the money, the quality and the time. That is a performance skill, and it is different from knowing. Most people who fail a lender interview knew the material; they had simply never said it aloud in one piece, in order, with a number in it, while someone waited for them to slip. You build it by rehearsing aloud, recording and scoring, and you prove it by doing better on the second recording than the first.

The mock interview

Imagine a senior construction lender and an experienced investor across the table. Read each question, answer aloud before you read the model answer, and be strict with yourself.

Question 1. How do you know the work you are paying for exists?

Answer: I never pay on the contractor's percentages. An independent cost consultant or the lender's monitor verifies each line, stored materials are paid only with title, insurance and segregation, and every month I report verified work in place, net paid and cost to complete side by side.

Question 2. The contractor wants to pour before the inspector arrives. What do you do?

Answer: I hold the pour. A hold point is released only by the named inspector, and photographs are not a substitute. A day of standing down costs a few thousand dollars; a pour over unverified work can cost many times that and the structure's credibility.

Question 3. A delay claim arrives for 30 days. How do you respond?

Answer: In writing. I check whether notice was given in time under the contract, ask for a time impact analysis showing the effect on the critical path, put my own decision log's dates beside the contractor's and have my cost consultant test the time-related costs. I neither dismiss it nor split it before it is analysed.

Question 4. How do you stop paying twice?

Answer: Lien waivers or releases with every payment, a title check before every draw, the statutory holdback where one applies, confirmed by local counsel, and no payment that leaves a subcontractor unpaid and able to claim against the land.

Question 5. When is the building substantially complete?

Answer: When the contract's definition is met, which in most forms means usable for its intended purpose. A building I cannot lawfully occupy because its integrated life-safety tests have not passed is not substantially complete, so retainage release and the transfer of risk wait for those tests.

Question 6. What does a 5 percent overrun do to your deal?

Answer: On a hypothetical 50,000,000-dollar project earning 3,500,000 dollars of NOI, 2,500,000 dollars of overrun lowers yield on cost from 7 to about 6.67 percent and removes more than a fifth of a 1.5-point development spread. If it comes with delay, the internal rate of return falls further, and any guarantee I signed puts the gap on my personal balance sheet.

Say that out loud now.

The recorded explanation

Now the real test. Set your phone to record, put it down where you cannot read from it and explain for three minutes how an owner controls a building under construction. Speak as if to a lender who has never met you. No notes.

When you stop, listen once and score yourself from 1 to 5 on four measures. Accuracy: were the facts and numbers right, and did you name the independent party at each link? Structure: did you open with the bottom line, move through the chain in order and close with a rule? Composure: pace, pauses and no apology for the subject. The hard question: did you answer, without being asked, the question a lender cares most about, which is how you know the work exists before you pay for it?

Write the four scores and the date in your decision journal. An example of honest scoring: if you said "the contractor manages quality" without naming hold points or who releases them, structure might still be a 4, but accuracy is a 2, because the phase's central idea is that someone independent verifies before anything is released.

Here is a model outline, about three minutes when spoken. One: "Building is a chain of proofs, and nothing is done, paid or accepted until someone independent verifies it." Two: "Setting out, ground, hold points, payment, completion." Three: "I pay only verified work, and I watch exposure, not budget." Four: "Every clock in the contract is on one register, and every notice is written." Five: "Completion follows integrated testing and lawful occupancy." Six: "Rule 123."

What to do with the scores

Any score of 3 or less points you back to a specific week. Accuracy errors on foundations and concrete send you to Weeks 110 to 113. Errors on payment and changes send you to Weeks 117 and 118 and this week's Day 3 and Day 5. Errors on closeout send you to Week 119. Weak structure means you rehearse the six-part outline twice and record again tomorrow. Composure improves fastest by recording often; the second recording is usually better than the first.

Rules I will not break

Below this lesson is the list of rules you have committed to so far, one from each failure case, now including Rule 123. Read each rule below aloud, then restate it in your own words. If you cannot restate a rule without looking, mark it and reread the lesson it came from this week.

A note on fairness to yourself. A first recording that scores 2s and 3s is normal and useful; it tells you exactly where to work. Keep both files, and listen to the first one again just before you record the next.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk at a checkpoint is scoring what you meant instead of what you said. The recording does not know what you meant. Score the tape.

The beginner's mistake

Reading the model answers instead of recording. Reading feels like mastery and proves little. Hearing yourself explain a build under pressure is the rehearsal that makes the real lender meeting familiar.

Callback

In Week 108, the design checkpoint asked how decisions lock in order. This phase asked how those decisions get built without losing what the design promised. Listen for whether your recording links them: a design with clear interface owners is easier to verify on site, and an owner who verifies on site protects what the design was paid to achieve.

Recap

Answer the six questions aloud. Record three minutes on how an owner controls a building under construction, score accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question from 1 to 5, and write the scores in your journal. Read every rule aloud and restate it.

checklist: RULES_SO_FAR
head: Rules I will not break
speak: An owner controls construction by keeping a chain of proofs intact. Nothing is done, paid or accepted until someone independent has verified it: the surveyor's control, the ground, the hold points in the inspection and test plan, payment against verified work and completion proved by integrated testing. I pay only what an independent consultant or the lender's monitor verifies, I exclude stored materials until title and insurance are proven, and I report exposure, not budget. I keep every notice period, holdback and warranty clock on one register, and every notice I send is in writing. A delay claim gets a request for analysis and my own dated records, not a reaction. Substantial completion follows integrated testing and lawful occupancy. And from this phase, Rule 123: I never let schedule pressure release a hold, and I never certify payment for work nobody independent has verified.
terms: Checkpoint — a scheduled test of whether a phase can be explained aloud under pressure, scored and recorded.
Decision journal — a dated written record of decisions, the reasons for them and the expected outcome, reviewed later against what happened.
Chain of verification — the sequence of independent checks, from setting out to completion, that must each be passed before the next step is released.

hostile.q: Your contractor is experienced and bonded. Why do you need to understand any of this?
hostile.a: Because the contractor builds the work, but I decide what gets released: each payment, each hold, each change and the completion certificate. A bond responds after a failure; it does not prevent one, and it does not cover my interest, my lost income or my guarantees. Knowing the chain of verification and who signs each link is how I keep cost, quality and time under my control.
